en: The *Paramalaghumañjūṣā* composed by the great grammarian Śrī Nāgeśabhaṭṭa,
accompanied by the Sanskrit-Hindi commentary *Kiraṇāvalī* composed by Ācārya Lokamaṇi Dāhāla.
Now, the determination of *śakti* (potency). Having bowed to Śiva, Nāgeśa has composed this irreproachable, supreme, and concise [work].
This *Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntamañjūṣā* is being composed. ||1||

In this regard, *sphoṭa* is threefold according to the distinction between phoneme (*varṇa*), word (*pada*), and sentence (*vākya*). Even there, it is further sixfold according to the distinction between genus (*jāti*) and individual (*vyakti*). Including the indivisible word-*sphoṭa* and the indivisible sentence-*sphoṭa*, there are eight *sphoṭas* in total. Among these, the sentence-*sphoṭa* is primary, because it alone conveys meaning in the world and because the purpose of communication is fulfilled by it alone. Thus says the author of the *Nyāyabhāṣya*: "A collection of words is a sentence when there is completion of the sense. The word "capable" (*samartha*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the definition].

In this regard, because it is impossible to grasp the linguistic convention for every individual sentence, and because the grammatical analysis of sentences cannot be accomplished by easy means, the teachers have—by means of conceptualization—divided sentences into words, and further divided words into bases and suffixes; then, through imagined methods of presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*), they have postulated the distinction between their respective meanings as a domain exclusive to the science of grammar.

The *varṇasphoṭa* is that which maintains the systematic framework (*prakriyā*) of the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*). Its purpose is to show that bases (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*) denote their respective meanings. Even the division into prefixes (*upasarga*), particles (*nipāta*), verbal roots (*dhātu*), and so forth, is merely conceptual. The substituends (*sthānin*), such as *la* and others, and the substitutes (*ādeśa*), such as *ti* and others, are themselves purely conceptual. In this regard, the meanings assigned by the sages to the substituends have been stated explicitly by them in their own words; however, the meanings of the substitutes are derived from the *Bhāṣya*, according to the principle that a substitute is only such if it is capable of expressing the meaning of its substituend.

And thus, the inquiry as to whether the denotative power (*vācakatva*) belongs to the substitutes (*ādeśas*) is entirely fruitless, because the imputed denotative power exists in both cases. However, primary denotative power resides in the word or sentence as a whole—whose form is conveyed through conceptual construction—since it is from that alone that people derive the understanding of meaning. According to the maxim, "The means for attaining the goal are not fixed," there is no harm even if the substituends (*sthānis*) differ according to different systems of grammar, just as there is no harm when scripts differ according to different regions. This is the general direction of the argument.

In that regard, Gautama’s Sūtra states: "The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony. And verbal testimony is a means of valid cognition in the form of instruction by a reliable person (āpta). A reliable person is one who possesses a complete ascertainment of the true nature of things through direct experience; he is one who does not speak otherwise even under the influence of passion and other such defects—so says Patañjali in the Caraka Saṃhitā.

With respect to a verbal cognition delimited by having as its object that which is delimited by a particular property (taddharma), the cause is the knowledge characterized by a relation (vṛtti) as determined by that same property. For this very reason, there is no verbal comprehension for one who has not grasped the relation. And for this very reason, the Bhāṣya on the *samartha*-sūtra is consistent: "For when 'guḍa' is uttered, sweetness is not understood as a qualifier. By words such as 'guḍa', the cognition produced is one whose qualifier is the genus (*jāti*), namely: "that which is delimited by the genus 'guḍatva' is the denotation of the word 'guḍa'."
Sweetness, however, is cognizable through another means of knowledge in the form of inference, such as: "Sugar is sweet because it is derived from sugarcane.

To exclude the possibility that a person who has grasped the word-potency (*śakti*) in a reversed relation of qualifier and qualified might derive from the word *ghaṭa* (pot) a cognition of a pot qualified by the universal *pot-ness* (*ghaṭatva*), the phrase "qualified by that property" (*taddharmāvacchinna*) is included. Furthermore, the relation of the occurrence (*vṛtti*) with respect to the cognition is to be understood as existing through two relations: (1) co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a manifested latent impression (*saṃskāra*) whose object is itself, and (2) having as its object the word that is the locus of that [occurrence].

Therefore, there is no comprehension for one who has not grasped the function (*vṛtti*), nor for one who has forgotten it, nor for one who does not know the word that expresses it; furthermore, there is no comprehension of the ether (*ākāśa*) presented as the substratum by the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*), nor of Caitra and others presented as the generator [of the cognition]. And as for the postulation of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), it is either simply the memory of the function already grasped, or it is the verbal cognition itself—this is another matter.
And that function is threefold: denotation (*śakti*), indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and suggestion (*vyañjanā*).

If it is asked, "What is the category of reality (padārtha) that constitutes *śakti* (power) in this context?"—the logicians (*tārkika*) maintain that it is the will of God (*īśvarecchā*), either in the form "this meaning is to be understood from this word" or "let this word convey this meaning"; for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), this very will is the power. That alone is the convention (*saṅketa*) and the relation (*sambandha*).

Although the relation characterized as "objectness" (viṣayatva) belongs equally to the word, the meaning, and the cognition, nevertheless, the expressive word (vācaka) is the object of the capacity by virtue of possessing a generative power (janakatā) that is defined by a producedness (janyatā) residing in the cognition; and the expressed meaning (vācya) is the object of the capacity by virtue of being the object of the cognition produced by the word. Thus, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Although the initial apprehension of the capacity occurs only in the sentence, they say that through the process of insertion and deletion (āvāpodvāpa) devised by the author of the grammatical treatise, the capacity of each individual word is apprehended.

That is not so; for since desire lacks the capacity to determine the substratum-hood (*āśrayatā*) of its two relata, it cannot possibly be a relation. This is because of the consensus of the learned that "a relation is that which, while being distinct from its two relata and residing in both, determines a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*) by way of being a substratum. For example, in cases such as "the ground possesses a jar," the relation in the form of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is distinct from the two relata, resides in both, and determines the qualified cognition: "the ground is the substratum of the conjunction as determined by the jar. However, desire does not fulfill these criteria.
In this context, there is no such conventional usage as "the word 'jar' possesses desire" or "its referent possesses desire.

Therefore, the relation between a word and its referent is indeed a distinct relation, synonymous with the terms *śakti* (potency) or *vācyavācakabhāva* (the relationship between the signified and the signifier). The apprehender of that [relation] is identity (*tādātmya*), which is rooted in mutual superimposition (*itaretarādhyāsa*). That alone is the relation, because of the linguistic usage regarding the referent and the word: "that which possesses the identity defined by both is neither [of them]. Furthermore, even in the case of a potency producing an effect, it is the relation itself that acts as the regulator.
For it is observed that although a lamp and the like possess the power of illumination, they illuminate objects only when there is a connection with light, and not otherwise. As it was said by Hari:
"Wherever that assistance exists, there the property is perceived."
"He is the power even of powers; he is the quality even of qualities. Regarding this:

where there exists a relationship characterized by assistance (*upakāra*) between the two capacities of cognition—the assisted (*upakārya*) and the assisting (*upakāra*)—there the property (*dharma*) in the form of a capacity (*śakti*) is inferred from the observation of its effect. This relationship assists even the capacities in the production of their effects, and it is also the regulator of the subsistence of qualities (*guṇa*) in substance (*dravya*), according to Helārāja.

That relationship exists both in the word (*pada*) and in the sentence (*vākya*). Thus says the author of the *Nyāyabhāṣya*: "Grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is the formal exposition of speech characterized by words for the sake of knowing the convention (*samaya*); it is the characterization of the meaning of speech characterized by sentences. By this, it is clearly stated that the convention of the Lord (*īśvara-samaya*) applies not only to words but also to sentences. Therefore, the collective meaning is that the relationship consists of mutual superimposition (*itaretarādhyāsa*), which is the convention (*saṅketa*), and the identity (*tādātmya*) rooted therein.
As it is said in the *Pātañjalabhāṣya*: [text follows].

The convention (*saṅketa*), however, consists of a mutual superimposition (*itaretarādhyāsa*) between the word and its object, having the nature of memory (*smṛtyātmaka*), such that "this word is this object" and "this object is this word.

By the term "having the nature of memory," it is shown that only a convention already known can serve as the indicator of the expressive power (*śakti*). Thus, the Nyāya position—that the convention of God alone is the expressive power—is not tenable; for the convention, expressed as "this [word] is denotable by this [object]" or "the expressive power of this [word] resides here [in the object]," is well-established as distinct from the expressive power itself. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Nyāyavācaspati*:

"The convention for the great seers and deities who exist from the beginning of creation was established directly by the Lord himself; and through their usage, that convention is easily grasped even by people such as ourselves."

In that identity (*tādātmya*), the intended object is called "capable" (*śakya*) by virtue of being the object of determination (*nirūpaka*), while the intended word is called "capable" (*śakta*) by virtue of being the locus (*āśraya*). Precisely because of this identity between word and meaning, there occurs such common usage as "he heard the verse," "then he hears the meaning," or "he speaks the meaning. Furthermore, there are instances of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the application of Vedic revelation (*śruti*) and traditional law (*smṛti*) which establish the expressive power (*śakti*), such as: "The single-syllabled Brahman is *Om*," "The two-syllabled name *Rāma* is the shatterer of the pride of the wielder of the Pināka bow," and "The term *vṛddhi* consists of *ā*, *ai*, and *au*."

Identity (*tādātmya*) consists in being perceived as non-different while remaining distinct; thus, it is co-extensive with both difference and non-difference. Furthermore, because non-difference is superimposed, there is no contradiction between the two. As for what the logicians (*tārkika*) say—that if identity were accepted between word and meaning, the tasting of sweetness would occur in the mouth upon uttering the word "honey," and burning would occur in the mouth upon uttering the word "fire"—that is not so, because difference and non-difference have been established.

In reality, it is the conceptual object (*boddha*) alone that is capable [of being denoted], and even the word is well-known to have the nature of *sphoṭa*. There is identity between these two. In that regard, since the conceptual object such as fire lacks the capacity for burning and so forth, the Sūtra on Conceptual Construction (*vikalpa*), which states, "Conceptual construction is that which follows from the cognition of a word and is devoid of a real object," is consistent. Its meaning is as follows: it "follows" (is dependent upon) the mere cognition of the word; it has the habit of "following after" in the intellect; it is "devoid of a real object," meaning it lacks an external referent; and it is "conceptually constructed" (*viśeṣeṇa kalpyate*), thus termed *vikalpa*—that is, it is a mental construct. Precisely for this reason: "This son of a barren woman goes, wearing a crest made of sky-flowers."
He has bathed in a pool of tortoise-milk and wields a bow made of rabbit-horn.

In this context, although the son of a barren woman (*vandhyā-suta*) and similar entities lack external reality, they possess nominal stem status (*prātipadikatva*) because they have semantic significance by taking up an object denoted by the word "son of a barren woman" as constructed by the intellect. Otherwise, due to the absence of semantic significance, there would be no nominal stem status, and consequently, the derivation of case endings (*svādi*) would not occur. As for the claim made by the logicians (*tārkika*) that in the expression "the horn of a hare" (*śaśa-śṛṅgam*), there is a misconception of the horn belonging to a hare—that is incorrect. For when there is a sublation consisting in the perception of the animal denoted by the word "hare," the phrase "the horn of a hare" would fail to attain nominal stem status within the sentence "the horn of a hare does not exist."

Because of the identity between the word and its meaning, the word—which has attained identity with each respective meaning—is distinct; for this reason, there is the conventional usage that "due to the difference in meanings, there is a difference in words. However, based merely on their identical form, there is the conventional usage that "this is one word having many meanings."

And that capacity exists in corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) just as it does in correct forms (*sādhu*), because linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), which is the preeminent means for grasping capacity, is equal in both cases. Through the observation of such usage, there occurs a recollection of the capacity experienced in a previous birth. For this very reason, children and even animals possess an understanding of syntactic relations (*anvaya-bodha*). It is not possible for them to acquire that understanding at that very moment [of first hearing]. As for what the logicians (*tārkika*) say—that the meaning is understood through a corrupt word by means of the recollection of the corresponding correct word—that is incorrect;

for we experience understanding even without the recollection of the correct word, and it would follow that understanding could not occur for those who do not know the correct word that expresses that meaning.

Nor should it be said that "understanding arises from corrupt words due to a delusion regarding their expressive power (*śakti*)," because a cognition free from doubt cannot be considered an error in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*). For this very reason, when a correct word is uttered by women, Śūdras, children, and others, if there is a doubt regarding its meaning, the meaning is determined through its corresponding corrupt form (*apabhraṃśa*). Consequently, the *Bhāṣya*—"When the comprehension of meaning is the same, the scripture [prescribes] a restriction of merit (*dharma*) regarding words and corrupt words"—and the verse of Hari—"Even though there is no difference in their capacity to denote (*vācakatva*), there is a restriction concerning merit and demerit"—are both consistent.

For this very reason, the section concerning Aryas and Mlecchas is consistent. For in that case, although the Aryas employ the word *yava* for long-awned barley (*dīrghaśūka*), while the Mlecchas employ it for the *priyaṅgu* plant and understand it as such, nevertheless, because the usage of the Aryas is stronger, it was concluded that in the Veda the term refers exclusively to long-awned barley.

However, since your understanding of the Mlecchas is rooted in a confusion regarding their powers (*śakti*), the Mleccha convention—being like a cognition of silver with respect to an object that is not actually silver—is incapable of establishing the reality of the thing. Therefore, it is quite clear that an investigation into which of the two conventions—that of the Āryas or that of the Mlecchas—is more authoritative is entirely misplaced. Furthermore, "correctness" (*sādhutva*) consists either in being derivable through grammar (*vyākaraṇa-anvākhyeyatva*) or in possessing a property that delimits the production of merit (*puṇya-janakatā-avacchedaka-dharma-vattva*). "Incorrectness" (*asādhutva*) is simply the state of being different from that.

And that power (śakti) is threefold: *rūḍhi* (convention), *yoga* (etymology), and *yogarūḍhi* (both convention and etymology). *Rūḍhi* is the power defined by the collective meaning of a word when there is no basis for the meanings of its constituent parts as conceived by the scriptures; for example, in the case of words such as *maṇinūpura* ("jeweled anklet"). *Yoga* is the power defined by the meanings of the constituent parts as conceived by the scriptures; for example, in the case of words such as *pācaka* ("cook"). *Yogarūḍhi* is the power defined by the meaning of the substantive element conjoined with the meanings of the constituent parts as conceived by the scriptures; for example, in the word *paṅkaja* ("lotus"). In this case, the cognition arises that "the lotus is the agent of arising from mud."

In the case of *padma*, there is no occasion for *lakṣaṇā* (indication) without the connection of non-origination (*anupapatti*) and the reconnection of relations (*sambandha-pratisandhāna*). In some instances, however, due to the force of an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*), there is the cognition of either the purely conventional (*rūḍhi*) meaning or the purely etymological (*yoga*) meaning, as in "A lotus has grown on the ground" and "Among the *paṅkajas* such as the *kahlāra* and *kairava*. This is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ārhād-aḥ*.

The word *aśvagandhā* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as a specific medicinal herb; yet, due to its possession of a scent associated with horses, it is etymologically derived (*yaugika*) when understood as a horse-stable. This is called "etymologically derived-conventional" (*yaugikarūḍha*). Similarly, the word *maṇḍapa* is conventionally established as a particular type of house, while it is etymologically derived when referring to one who performs the act of eating.

This very power (*śakti*) is restricted to various meanings by means of association (*saṃyoga*) and other factors. As it was said by Bhartṛhari: "Association, dissociation, companionship, opposition,"
The meaning, the context, the indicative mark, and the proximity of another word.
"Capability, propriety, place, time, gender, accent, and so forth,
are the causes for the recollection of a specific meaning when there is no determination of a word's meaning.

This means that these factors— conjunction and the rest— when a word with multiple meanings has its sense undetermined or ambiguous, serve to determine the specific meaning by way of removing that doubt.

The examples for conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*viprayoga*) are "the cow with its calf" and "the cow without its calf. The example for association (*sāhacarya*) is "Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa," because association is a form of similarity based on the rule that two similar things are used together. In cases such as "the movement of Rāma and Arjuna," it is determined by opposition (*virodha*). In the instances "he offers oblations with joined palms" and "he worships the sun with joined palms," the word *añjali* refers to the specific shape of the palms according to the requirements of the meaning of the words such as "offers oblations."

In such cases as "Bring the Saindhava," [the meaning is determined] by context (*prakaraṇa*). In "He places the smeared pebbles," the word *akta* (smeared) refers to anointing with ghee, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the praise of ghee: "Ghee is indeed brilliance. In "Rāma is the son of Jamadagni," [it is understood that] Rāma is Paraśurāma due to the proximity (*sannidhāna*) of the word "son of Jamadagni. In "A maiden should be given to one who is handsome," it is understood from the capacity (*sāmarthya*) that she is to be given to one who is most handsome. And: "Whether one cuts a neem tree with an axe, or another with honey and ghee, or yet another with perfumes, garlands, and the like—the tree remains bitter for everyone."

In this context, by virtue of propriety (*aucitya*), the word *paraśunā* (with an axe) has the sense of cutting; *madhusarpiṣā* (with honey and ghee) has the sense of sprinkling; and *gandhamālyādyaiḥ* (with perfumes, garlands, etc. has the sense of worship. In the phrase "The Supreme Lord shines here," because the location is a royal capital, the term *parameśvara* indicates a king. In expressions such as "Citrabhānu shines," it refers to fire at night and the sun during the day. Gender (*liṅga*) [is a determinant]: in cases such as *mitro bhāti* (the friend shines) and *mitraṃ bhāti* (the sun shines), it is the sun in the first instance and a well-wisher in the latter. In the case of *sthūlapṛṣatīm*, the determination of whether it is a *tatpuruṣa* or a *bahuvrīhi* compound is made from the accent (*svara*).
Thus ends the determination of *śakti* (denotative power). Now follows the determination of *lakṣaṇā* (indicative power).

If it is asked, "What is the nature of the category of *lakṣaṇā*?", the logicians (*tārkikas*) maintain here that indicative power is a relation with that which is directly denoted by the word itself (*sva-śakya-sambandha*). And it is of two kinds: metaphorical (*gauṇī*) and pure (*śuddhā*).

The figurative (gauṇī) [metaphorical] function is that which conveys a meaning related to the primary meaning through the relation of being the locus of similarity with its own form (*svanirūpatisādṛśyādhikaraṇatva*). The pure (*śuddhā*) [metaphorical] function is that which conveys a meaning related to the primary meaning through a relation other than that.

That [metaphor] is also twofold in another way: *ajahatsvārthā* (non-abandoning its own meaning) and *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning). *Ajahatsvārthā* is that which expresses another meaning while being conjoined with its own meaning. Thus, in cases such as "the umbrella-bearers go," "bring in the spears," "bring in the sticks," and "let the curd be protected from crows," there arises the cognition of an army accompanied by umbrella-bearers, of men accompanied by weapons in the form of spears, of men accompanied by sticks, and of all things that destroy curd including crows. The latter (*jahatsvārthā*) is that which expresses another meaning by abandoning its own meaning.

And that abandonment [of the primary meaning] consists in the fact that the literal sense is not connected with that which is connected with the indicated sense. Therefore, in cases such as "Teach the Vāhīka the cow," even when there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of one who resembles a cow, the literal sense—the cow—is not connected with the action of teaching that is connected with the indicated sense.

And that indication is based on such grounds as "being located therein" (*tātsthyāt*). As it has been said: "On account of being located therein, likewise on account of possessing its qualities (*tāddharmyāt*), and likewise on account of proximity (*tatsāmīpyāt*)."

"Through association with that, through being for the sake of that, the figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) should indeed be understood by the wise. Thus: through location (*tātsthyāt*), as in "the platforms laugh" or "the village has fled"; through possession of its qualities (*tāddharmyāt*), as in "the boy is a lion" or "the Vāhīka is an ox"; through proximity (*tatsāmīpyāt*), as in "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā"; through association (*tatsāhacaryāt*), as in "bring in the staffs" [meaning the persons carrying them]; and through being for the sake of that (*tādarthyāt*), as in "the pillar for Indra is Indra."

The awareness of the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*) is the seed of indication (*lakṣaṇā*). In reality, however, the seed of that [indication] is precisely the awareness of the impossibility of the intended meaning (*tātparyānupapatti*). Otherwise, in cases such as "A hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), there would result an indication of crocodiles and the like in the word "hamlet" itself, since the syntactic connection would be resolved by that much alone. Furthermore, in cases such as "A sinner goes to the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ pāpī gacchati*), there would result an indication of hell for the word "Ganges. For us, however, there is no fault, because the intention is that [the word] indicates one who is delimited by past sins.

In the case of the statement "Having seen the constellation, one should utter speech," even though a literal connection (*anvaya*) is possible, metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is nevertheless accepted precisely because the intended meaning (*tātparya*) would otherwise be untenable; furthermore, when the purpose can be achieved by accepting a single unifying factor, it is more cumbersome to accept multiple such factors.

The elders employ the term *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (indication with partial abandonment) for the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a word denoting a qualified object upon a single part of that object's referent (*padārtha*). This involves the abandonment of certain aspects of the literal meaning and the acceptance of other aspects. In this regard, when a part of a village or a part of a cloth is burned, there arises the common usage: "The village is burned" or "The cloth is burned. In the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), there is the abandonment of omniscience and limited knowledge [respectively], and the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of pure consciousness as non-different.

Some maintain that indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is the relation between the thing to be understood by the word itself (*svabodhya*) and [the indicated object]. This is in accordance with examples such as "a hamlet on the deep river" (*gabhīrāyāṃ nadyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*). To explain: first of all, the word *gabhīra* ("deep") cannot indicate the bank, because that would result in a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the word *nadyām* ("on the river"). For the bank is not the river. For this very reason, it cannot be the word *nadī* either, because the meaning of the word *gabhīra* would then fail to connect [with it]. For the bank is not deep. Nor can indication reside in each of the two words individually, because that would fail to produce the cognition of a river qualified by depth. Therefore, the thing to be understood by the composite expression is the river qualified by depth; the relation to that [qualified entity] is indication.

When there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *dvirepha* upon its own indicated object, namely the meaning expressed by the word "bee" (*bhramara*), it is conventionally termed "indication of the indicated" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*). The relation [between the primary and secondary meanings] is the state of being the denoted object of a word that is itself understood [by the primary meaning]. Furthermore, indication is of two kinds by another classification; as follows:

"It is held that indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is of two kinds: purposeful (*prayojanavatī*) and conventional (*rūḍhā*). When there is no purpose, the connection with the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*) is called conventional indication, as in "known by the skin" (*tvacā jñātam*), where "skin" refers to the sense-organ of touch (*tvagindriya*). It should be understood, however, that this [conventional indication] is synonymous with the primary meaning itself. In the example "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), the purpose is the cognition of coolness, purity, and so forth, which belong to the Gaṅgā, as perceived in the bank. In "the Vāhīka is a cow" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*), similarity is the delimiting factor of the indicated object (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), and the cognition of non-difference from a cow is the purpose.

Regarding the statement "The spears enter," they say that in a sentence spoken by those fleeing out of fear, the purpose is the cognition of the sharpness residing in the spears as it pertains to the persons qualified by those spears.

That is not so. For when there is an intention [to convey a specific meaning], there is no secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) because of the Bhāṣya statement, "all words denote all things. Furthermore, it would involve the complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating two distinct delimiters for two distinct functions, and it is improper to postulate a secondary function when a primary one is available. [Objection: How then does the cognition of a riverbank arise from a word such as *gaṅgā*? [Reply: You are mistaken. Accept the Bhāṣya itself: "all words denote all things," provided there is an intention [to convey that meaning]. To explain: power (*śakti*) is of two kinds—well-known (*prasiddha*) and unknown (*aprasiddha*).

Being cognizable by those of dull intellect is "well-known" (*prasiddhatva*); being cognizable by the sensitive alone (*sahṛdaya-mātra*) is "not well-known" (*aprasiddhatva*). In this regard, what is inconsistent about the fact that the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of words such as *gaṅgā* is well-known with respect to the current and the like, yet not well-known with respect to the bank and the like?

If you say, "Surely all words denote all objects," then why would there not be a cognition of a cloth from the word "pot"? If you ask this, we say no; for it has been stated that [a word denotes an object] "when there is an intention (tātparya). Understand that [the cognition does not arise] because of the absence of such an intention. And in this context, the intention is understood by us and others through the tradition of the Lord, the deities, the great seers, and the elders of the world. Thus, everything is well-established. This concludes the determination of *lakṣaṇā* (indication). Now follows the determination of *vyañjanā* (suggestion).

Now, what is the meaning of the term *vyañjanā*? It is said: *Vyañjanā* is a specific type of mental impression (*saṃskāra-viśeṣa*) that generates a cognition independently of the sublation of the primary meaning; it is common to both [meanings] related and unrelated to the primary meaning, has as its object both well-known and unknown meanings, and is awakened by the knowledge of the particularities of the speaker and other factors, as well as by intuition (*pratibhā*).

For this very reason, Hari and others have stated that particles (*nipāta*) possess the quality of being *dyotaka* (illuminators) and that the *sphoṭa* is what is manifested by them. Furthermore, the quality of being an illuminator consists in being the manifester of the power residing in the word with which it is uttered in proximity. This acceptance is necessary even for the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*). And this [power] exists everywhere—in words, their meanings, parts of words, phonemes, sentences, compositions, gestures, and so forth—because it is experienced exactly in that way.

Furthermore, the knowledge of the specific qualities of the speaker and other factors is an auxiliary cause for the comprehension of a particular suggested meaning (vyaṅgya); thus, it is not required in every instance, as is explained in detail elsewhere. As for what the logicians (tārkika) say—that "suggestion (vyañjanā) is already accounted for by indication (lakṣaṇā) and therefore need not be accepted"—that is incorrect; for indication functions by first negating the primary meaning (mukhyārtha) and then conveying a secondary meaning (lakṣyārtha), and indication conveys only that meaning which is related to the primary meaning. Since suggestion does not function in this way, it cannot be subsumed under it. This is the direction of the argument. Thus ends the investigation into suggestion. Now begins the definition of the Sphoṭa.

Now, what is this word that is the substratum of the mental mode (*vṛtti*)? If it is argued that it is the individual phonemes (*varṇa*), that cannot be so; for otherwise, the utterance of the second and subsequent phonemes would be rendered useless. Nor can it be a collection of phonemes; because, since they perish as soon as they are uttered, simultaneity is impossible. Furthermore, whether considered as manifestations or as productions, phonemes exist for only a moment; and since time consisting of moments is not amenable to perception, a phoneme delimited by such time is likewise imperceptible.

The state of having perished immediately after the time of its utterance (*uccaritapradhvaṃsitva*) consists in being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of a destruction that occurs at a time subsequent to the locus of its utterance. Furthermore, in rules such as *iko yaṇ aci*, since the meaning of the sentence is supplemented by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) *tasmin* [iti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya], it would be impossible to employ the discourse of priority and posteriority—such as "this is prior" or "this is posterior"—with respect to what has perished, using the word *idam* (this) as the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

As for what the logicians say: even though letters are impermanent, the property of preceding letters in each succeeding letter is apprehended by virtue of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) through the relation of "immediate succession"; thus, because the word (*pada*) is perceived, there is verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). Alternatively, sounds produced by each preceding letter arise according to the principle of "sound-born sound" until the perception of the final letter; thus, there is no impossibility of perceiving the word.
Or else, verbal comprehension arises from the experience of the final letter conjoined with the mental impressions produced by the experiences of the preceding letters. This is what they claim.

That is not so. In the first case, because the desire to express "this is the former" and "this is the latter" is impossible, a relation of immediate succession (*avyavahitottaratva*) cannot be established. Furthermore, it is impossible to speak of a relation of immediate succession between that which has perished and that which exists. In the second case, even if the perception of a word (*pada*) is accounted for through the logic of sound produced by sound (*śabdaja-śabda*), since the word is no longer present, it is impossible to apprehend its status as the locus of expressive power (*śakti*). Moreover, if one were to admit the status of being a locus for something non-existent, it would lead to such absurdities as "the destroyed pot contains water."

In the third [view], since there is no determining factor (*vinigamaka*) for the claim that the impression (*saṃskāra*) of a word resides in the same sequence as its experience, there would arise the undesirable consequence of the cognition of individual alternative meanings in cases such as *sarorasaḥ* and *nadī dīnaḥ*, due to the awakening of contrary impressions. Furthermore, if the word—consisting of a collection of phonemes (*varṇa*)—were distinct [for each utterance] like a human being or other entities, characterized by arising and perishing, this would contradict the Bhāṣya which states: "The single word *indra* manifested at a hundred sacrifices becomes a constituent part (*aṅga*) in all sacrifices simultaneously.
Here, "manifested" (*prādurbhūtaḥ*) means "made manifest" (*abhivyaktaḥ*).

Now, what then is the word that is the substratum of the manifestation (*vṛtti*)? Understand it to be of the nature of *sphoṭa*. But what is this *sphoṭa*? It is said: speech (*vāc*) is indeed fourfold—*parā*, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*. Among these, that which resides in the *mūlādhāra*, which has been refined by the vital air (*pavana*) located in the *mūlādhāra*, which is the form of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*), devoid of vibration (*spanda*), and consisting of the *bindu*, is called *parā* speech. That which is manifested by the air reaching as far as the navel and which becomes the object of the mind is called *paśyantī* speech.

These two constitute the Word-Brahman (*vāgbrahma*), which is said to be the object of both non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*) knowledge in the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of yogis. Then, as that breath reaches as far as the heart, it manifests the *sphoṭa*—the form of the word denoting various meanings—which, being subtle and incapable of being grasped by the ear, is perceivable only by the intellect during recitation and such; this is called *madhyamā* speech.

Thereafter, as that breath moves upward and reaches as far as the mouth, it strikes the crown of the head, turns back, and is manifested in the respective articulatory locations (*sthāna*); this is called *vaikharī* speech, which is perceivable even by the ears of others.
Thus it is said:
"The supreme speech (parā-vāk) resides in the mūlādhāra-cakra; the visionary speech (paśyantī) is situated in the navel;
the intermediate speech (madhyamā) is to be known as residing in the heart; and the articulate speech (vaikharī) is located in the region of the throat."
"For the sound produced by *vaikharī* is within the range of hearing for others;

the sound produced by *madhyamā* is said to be the manifester of the *sphoṭa*. Thus it is said. Furthermore, when sound is produced by both *madhyamā* and *vaikharī*, therein the *madhyamā*-sound denotes the meaning and manifests the word whose essence is the *sphoṭa*. The *vaikharī*-sound is mere resonance (*dhvani*), perceptible by the ears of all people, and like the sound of a drum or similar instruments, it is devoid of meaning. The *madhyamā*-sound, moreover, is subtler; when the ears are closed or during silent recitation (*japa*), it is manifested by a subtler vital air and serves as the manifester of the *sphoṭa* which is the nature of the Word-Brahman (*śabda-brahman*).
Even within such [manifestations], the word whose essence is *sphoṭa* is unmanifested, of the nature of Brahman, and eternal.
Thus Hari said:
"Brahman, which is without beginning or end, is the imperishable reality of sound (*śabdatattva*)."
"From which the process of world-creation evolves in the form of objects. Thus [it is said].

And although that [sphoṭa] is one and indivisible, nevertheless—just as a crystal appears red or yellow due to the influence of the coloring (uparāga) of manifesting factors such as a hibiscus flower or a yellow substance—it likewise appears in the form of phonemes, words, or sentences, being manifested by the phonemes and so forth. And just as in a face there is the appearance of length, roundness, and so on, due to the influence of manifesting conditions such as a gem, a sword, or a mirror, so it is here. As it has been said:
"In a word, phonemes do not exist; nor do parts exist in phonemes.
There is no absolute distinction whatsoever between words and a sentence."

Furthermore, properties such as *katva* (the quality of being *ka*) and *gatva* (the quality of being *ga*), which reside in the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*), appear in the *sphoṭa*. This is because in the world, a reflection is perceived only through its qualification by the properties residing in the original object (*bimba*), and because a crystal or similar medium appears only as determined by its manifesting agent. This is just as the single ether has a conditional distinction as "the ether of a jar" (*ghaṭākāśa*) or "the great ether" (*mahākāśa*), and just as the single conscious principle has a conditional distinction as the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), as well as the mutual distinction among individual souls.

Thus, because properties such as *katva* (the quality of being *ka*) residing in the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*) are perceived within the *sphoṭa*, the linguistic usage of distinction—such as "the letter *ka* is cognized"—is merely conditional (*aupādhika*). Regarding this "conditional distinction," the intended meaning is that while the conditions (*upādhi*), such as *katva* and so forth, are distinct, the substratum (*upadheya*)—namely, the ether-like *sphoṭa* and so on—is one and the same. However, according to the view that words and sentences possess parts (*sakhaṇḍatvapakṣa*), the *sphoṭa* manifested by the final phoneme is indeed one; the preceding phonemes, meanwhile, serve to apprehend the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*), just as the word "variegated" (*citra*) does in the Nyāya system in expressions such as "owner of variegated cows" (*citragu*).

Sound (*dhvani*), however, is of two kinds: the primary (*prākṛta*) and the modified (*vaikṛta*). The first, the primary, is that which is produced by nature—that is, by the desire to convey meaning or by its own inherent character—and serves to manifest the *sphoṭa*. That which is born from this primary sound, characterized by modification, enduring for a longer duration, and causing [the manifestation] to cease, is the modified (*vaikṛta*). Hari also says: "The primary sound is held to be the cause for the perception of the word;
but the modified sounds function after the manifestation of the word, in the differentiation of its modes."
"The sounds (dhvanis) bring about the manifestation; the essence of the sphoṭa is not differentiated by them. Thus [it is said].
The remainder [of the statement] is that after the manifestation of the sound, modified sounds (*dhvani*) arise. Regarding the "distinction of tempos" (*vṛttibheda*):
"The fast tempo (*drutā vṛtti*) is for the purpose of practice; likewise, the medium tempo (*madhyā*) is for reflection;
and the slow tempo (*vilambitā*) is desired for the instruction of disciples. Thus it is said.
The meaning is that while the causes converge within the three modes of operation, the *sphoṭa* itself is not differentiated by them.

In this regard, the following should be understood: someone utters the articulated sound (*vaikharī-nāda*) "Bring the jar. That sound is perceived by another through the sense of hearing. Having reached the intellect and the heart via the sense organ, that sound manifests the word which conveys the meaning through its own inherent nature and so forth; from that, the comprehension of the meaning arises. It is called *sphoṭa* based on the etymology "that from which the meaning bursts forth (*sphuṭati*). For the speaker, however, the sound is produced simultaneously by both the intermediate (*madhyamā*) and the articulated (*vaikharī*) stages.

In this context, the *vaikharī* sound, like the blowing of a fire, is the stimulator of the *madhyamā* sound. The *madhyamā* sound manifests the *sphoṭa*, whereby the comprehension of meaning occurs immediately; for it is established by experience that for another [the listener], there is a delay. For this very reason, the traditional texts are consistent in stating: "Sound is that which is perceived by the ear, is grasped by the intellect, is manifested through effort, and occupies the space of ether. Its being perceived by the ear is due to its qualities such as *katva* (the quality of *k*), while its being grasped by the intellect is in the form of words and so forth, which are essentially *sphoṭa*.

And its meaning is this: by means of application (*prayoga*), it is ignited in the form of *vaikharī* and rendered manifest in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). In that context as well, just as in the case of denotability (*śakyatva*), the denotative power (*vācakatva*) belongs to the genus (*jāti*) residing in the phonemes, words, and sentences, which serves as the delimiting factor for the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedikā*).
As it has been said: "The genus manifested by many individuals is known as *sphoṭa*.

Therefore, sound (*śabda*), consisting of the eightfold *sphoṭa*, is the substratum of the linguistic function (*vṛtti*). In reality, however, it is specifically the sentence-*sphoṭa* or the sentence-genus-*sphoṭa* that is the substratum of the function; for it has been stated that from that alone arises the comprehension of meaning in the world, and thus everything is well-established.

Thus concludes the investigation of *sphoṭa*. Now follows the examination of *ākāṅkṣā* (expectancy). Next, the auxiliary causes of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) are expectancy, compatibility (*yogyatā*), contiguity (*āsatti*), and intentionality (*tātparya*). Expectancy is that which grasps the conventional relation (*samaya*) of a sentence. It is a desire for an object of knowledge, occurring when there is a cognition of the meaning of one word, directed toward the cognition of another meaning capable of being syntactically connected with it; its form is "What is the meaning that connects with this? and it resides solely in the person. Nevertheless, it is superposed upon its own object, the meaning, because of the common usage: "This meaning expects another meaning. This very state is called the "non-termination of the denotative function" (*abhidhānaparyavasāna*).

However, there is no requirement [of expectancy] regarding the word itself, because expectancy arises only after the meaning has been understood. The statement "a word is expectant" (sākāṅkṣa) means that it conveys an expectant meaning. As it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the *Samartha-sūtra*: "Some say that mutual dependence (*vyapekṣā*) is semantic competency (*sāmarthya*). But what is this mutual dependence between two words? We do not say 'between two words'; rather, we say 'between two meanings'."

And that which arouses such an inquiry is the knowledge that, with respect to one word-meaning, there is an absence of the generation of a cognition of syntactic connection (anvaya-bodha) when another word-meaning is absent; thus, even though there is an absence of such a cognition of syntactic connection regarding that object [the word-meaning], it is conventionally designated as "expectancy" (ākāṅkṣā).

Alternatively, expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is the desire to know another object, related either by the relation of being an arouser (*utthāpakatā*) or by the relation of being its object (*viṣayatā*), or by both relations together. In the first case, in the sentence "Look, the deer runs," the meaning of the act of seeing possesses the quality of being an arouser of the expectancy for the agent's running, while the running itself is indeed its object. In the second case, however, in sentences such as "Devadatta cooks rice," both the action and the agent possess the quality of being mutual arousers of expectancy for one another, yet neither is the object of the other.

Therefore, from the expression "the pot, the objectness, bringing, effort," there is no comprehension of syntactic relation (*anvayabodha*), just as there is none from "bring the pot," because of the absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). This is because only those [words] ending in case-terminations and verbal suffixes—such as "the pot" and "bring"—possess mutual expectancy. Thus concludes the investigation of expectancy.
Now follows the investigation of compatibility (*yogyatā*).

Competence (*yogyatā*) is the possession of a property that serves as the cause for mutual syntactic connection (*anvaya*). By this standard, the sentence "He sprinkles with water" (*payasā siñcati*) is competent. For competence—in the form of being a liquid substance (*dravadravyatva*), which is the cause for its connection with the act of sprinkling—exists in water. Competence—in the form of moistening (*ārdrīkaraṇatva*), which is the cause for water's connection [with the act] as an instrument (*karaṇatva*)—exists in the act of sprinkling. For this very reason, the sentence "He sprinkles with fire" (*vahninā siñcati*) is incompetent, because fire lacks the quality of being a liquid substance, which is the cause for its connection with the act of sprinkling.

The Naiyāyikas maintain that in such instances there is no cognition of syntactic relation (anvaya), but rather merely the cognition of each individual word-meaning; however, this is not correct. For in all cases, it is the conceptual object (bauddhārtha) alone that is the object of cognition, and thus there is no contradiction [with experience]. As Haribhadra also said:
"For even with respect to an object that is absolutely non-existent, a word produces a cognition."

Therefore, even words such as "son of a barren woman" possess the status of nominal stems (*prātipadika*). Furthermore, if there were no cognition arising from the sentence "He sprinkles with fire," then mockery directed at the speaker of that sentence—such as "How can you speak of sprinkling with fire, which is not liquid?"—would not be possible. Once the understanding of the sentence-meaning has arisen, activity toward the mentally conceived object does not occur, because unreliability (*aprāmāṇya*) is apprehended regarding that mentally conceived object; this is explained in detail elsewhere.
Thus concludes the investigation into semantic competency (*yogyatā*).
Now follows the investigation into contiguity (*āsatti*).

*Āsatti* (proximity) is the non-intervention of words that are conducive to the comprehension of the intended syntactic connection (*anvaya*). For example, "girir agnimān agniḥ" ("the mountain has fire; fire") is proximate. Conversely, "girir bhuktam agnimān devadattena" ("the mountain, [Devadatta] ate, possesses fire") is not proximate. Proximity is also a cause for the unimpeded verbal cognition of one with dull intellect. However, for one of sharp intellect, even in the absence of proximity, cognition occurs without delay once the word-meanings are presented through expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors; thus, it is not a cause for cognition in their case. This has been indicated in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "na padānta... (Pāṇini 8.4.39).

In expressions such as "he cooks rice in a pot" (*sthālyām odanaṃ pacati*), even though the word *sthālyām* is separated from the word *odana*, there is no loss of proximity (*āsatti*) because it is conducive to the comprehension of the intended syntactic connection. This concludes the determination of proximity. Now follows the investigation into intention (*tātparya*).

*Taṭparya* (intention) is the will of God (*īśvarecchā*) that "this sentence or this word should be uttered for the sake of communicating this particular meaning. For this very reason, it has been stated that according to the grammarians' doctrine—that "all words denote all meanings"—there is no cognition of a cloth from the word "jar" when *taṭparya* is present. In the case of words with multiple meanings (*nānārtha*), however, in common worldly usage, *taṭparya* consists of the speaker's intention in the form: "I am uttering this word or sentence for the purpose of conveying this specific meaning. And in the world, the determinants of *taṭparya* are context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth.

Therefore, when it is said during a meal, "Bring some *saindhava*," the word *saindhava* conveys the idea of salt; yet at the time of battle, it conveys the idea of a horse. And in the case of Vedic sentences, the understanding of the meaning arises from the intention of the Lord (*īśvara*).

[Objection: If context and the other factors are the determinants of word-potency (*śakti*), then since the purpose is already served by potency alone, what is the use of *tātparya* (intentional import)? [Reply: This is not so, because there is a contradiction with such experience as: "From this word, a cognition arises having two objects as its qualifiers, since potency exists toward both objects; yet we do not know which of the two is the intended one. For this very reason, when it is said, "Bring the *payas*," a question from someone who does not know the context—asking whether "milk or water should be brought"—is appropriate. Thus ends the investigation into *tātparya*.
